sections.section_title: Contraception in women with medical conditions

blocks.text: You may be asked to:
Counsel a woman with hypertension who wants contraception.
Choose contraception for a patient with migraine with aura.
Advise a woman with a history of deep-vein thrombosis (DVT) or pulmonary embolism (PE).
Counsel a patient with diabetes mellitus.
Recommend contraception for a woman living with HIV or taking antiretroviral therapy.
Advise a woman with epilepsy who is taking anti-seizure medication.
Counsel a woman with breast cancer or significant liver disease.
Select contraception for a woman with obesity, smoking history or multiple cardiovascular risk factors.

Main OSCE objective: identify the medical condition, assess its severity and associated risks, apply medical eligibility criteria, and recommend a safe, effective method that respects the patient's preferences.

“Hello, my name is Dr ____. I understand you would like advice about contraception, and that you have a medical condition that may affect which methods are suitable. I will ask a few questions about your health and medications, then explain the options, their benefits and risks. We can choose a method together. Is that okay?”
Maintain a non-judgemental approach. Do not automatically deny contraception because a patient has a chronic illness.
Ask about:
Last menstrual period and menstrual regularity.
Possibility of current pregnancy.
Previous pregnancies and complications.
Current contraceptive method and reason for changing it.
Future pregnancy plans and preferred duration of contraception.
Clarify:
The specific diagnosis and its duration.
Disease severity and whether it is controlled.
Previous complications, hospitalisations or relevant surgery.
Other cardiovascular or metabolic conditions.
Current medications, including over-the-counter and herbal products.
Ask whether the patient prefers:
A long-acting reversible method.
A daily pill.
An injectable method.
A hormone-free option.
Condoms for STI protection.
Permanent contraception, if appropriate and desired.
Perform examinations or request investigations when indicated by the history or proposed method.
Examples include:
Blood pressure before prescribing combined hormonal contraception.
Pregnancy testing when pregnancy cannot reasonably be excluded.
Assessment of VTE risk where relevant.
Review of glucose control and vascular complications in diabetes.
Medication reconciliation for enzyme-inducing drug interactions.
OSCE principle: do not order unnecessary investigations or delay a suitable contraceptive method when investigations are not required for safe initiation.
The WHO and other national guidelines use medical eligibility categories to guide contraceptive choice.

rows: Advantages generally outweigh theoretical or proven risks
Risks generally outweigh advantages; use only when more appropriate methods are unavailable or unacceptable, with clinical judgement
Unacceptable health risk; do not use

blocks.text: The category applies to a specific contraceptive method in a specific medical condition. It is not a blanket category for all contraception.
For example, a woman with hypertension may be unsuitable for combined hormonal contraception but may still be eligible for a progestogen-only method or an intrauterine device.
Oestrogen-containing contraception can increase cardiovascular risk, particularly in women with severe or uncontrolled hypertension.

rows: Usually avoid combined hormonal contraception where safer alternatives are suitable; assess eligibility carefully
Combined hormonal contraception is generally not recommended under commonly used medical eligibility criteria
Combined hormonal contraception is contraindicated under commonly used criteria

blocks.text: Preferred options to consider: copper IUD, levonorgestrel IUS, implant or progestogen-only pill, depending on individual eligibility.
OSCE question: Why is combined hormonal contraception a concern in hypertension?
Because oestrogen-containing methods can increase the risk of stroke, myocardial infarction and other cardiovascular complications in susceptible patients.
Clinical note: confirm properly measured blood pressure and apply the current local medical eligibility guidance. A single elevated reading alone does not establish chronic hypertension.
The key distinction is whether the patient experiences migraine with aura.
Combined hormonal contraception may be considered in selected patients after assessment of age, smoking, blood pressure and other stroke risks.
Combined hormonal contraception is contraindicated under commonly used eligibility criteria because of increased ischaemic stroke risk.
Preferred alternatives: progestogen-only pill, implant, copper IUD or LNG-IUS, subject to other medical factors.
OSCE tip: ask about visual disturbances, flashing lights, zigzag lines, sensory symptoms or speech disturbance preceding the headache. Do not assume every severe headache is migraine with aura.

content_groups.group_title: C. Previous DVT or pulmonary embolism

blocks.text: Oestrogen increases the risk of venous thromboembolism.
Ask about:
Previous DVT or PE.
Whether the event was provoked or unprovoked.
Recurrent thrombosis or known thrombophilia.
Current anticoagulant treatment.
Family history of early or recurrent thrombosis.

rows: Often suitable; may reduce heavy menstrual bleeding
Often suitable, depending on individual eligibility
Generally avoided in patients with significant VTE risk; may be contraindicated

blocks.text: Important: eligibility can differ according to whether the patient has active VTE, is receiving anticoagulation, has a history of thrombosis or has thrombophilia. Consult the relevant guideline rather than treating all cases identically.
Examiner question: What if the patient is taking anticoagulants and has heavy menstrual bleeding?

The LNG-IUS may be a useful option because it can reduce menstrual blood loss, provided it is appropriate for the individual patient. Insertion planning should account for the anticoagulant and bleeding history.
The main issue is whether the patient has uncomplicated diabetes or vascular complications.
Many contraceptive methods are suitable. Choice depends on the patient's preferences and other risks.
Examples include:
Nephropathy.
Retinopathy.
Neuropathy.
Other established vascular disease.
Combined hormonal contraception may be unsuitable, particularly with longstanding diabetes or multiple cardiovascular risk factors.
Options to consider: copper IUD, LNG-IUS, implant or progestogen-only pill, according to eligibility.
OSCE tip: ask about disease duration, glucose control, kidney disease, eye complications, hypertension, smoking and cardiovascular history.
The diagnosis of epilepsy alone does not automatically preclude contraception. The important issue is the medication.
Some enzyme-inducing anti-seizure medicines can reduce the effectiveness of hormonal contraception, including:
Carbamazepine.
Phenytoin.
Phenobarbital.
Primidone.
Certain doses of topiramate.
Lamotrigine has a different interaction: combined hormonal contraception can lower lamotrigine concentrations, potentially affecting seizure control.
Options to consider:
Copper IUD.
LNG-IUS.
Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate in suitable patients, because its effectiveness is generally not reduced by enzyme induction.
Other methods after checking specific drug interactions and guidelines.
Examiner question: Why is the implant not always the best option in a patient taking carbamazepine?
Carbamazepine can increase the metabolism of implant hormones, reducing contraceptive effectiveness. An intrauterine method may be more reliable.
Never advise a patient to stop anti-seizure medication without specialist input.
Current breast cancer is a major contraindication to hormonal contraception under commonly used eligibility criteria.
Options to consider include:
Copper IUD, if appropriate.
Condoms.
Permanent contraception if desired.
Other non-hormonal approaches where suitable.
For a patient with a history of breast cancer, eligibility depends on the clinical circumstances and guideline. Involve the treating oncology team when necessary.
OSCE tip: do not automatically recommend an implant, hormonal IUS or progestogen-only pill simply because it contains no oestrogen. These are still hormonal methods.
Obesity alone does not automatically exclude most contraceptive methods.
However, assess additional risks:
Hypertension.
Smoking.
Migraine with aura.
Diabetes and vascular disease.
Previous VTE.
Reduced mobility or recent surgery.
Combined hormonal contraception may be inappropriate when obesity is accompanied by significant additional cardiovascular or thrombotic risks.
The implant and intrauterine methods are highly effective options to discuss. Do not assume that a patient with obesity cannot use hormonal contraception.
Combined hormonal contraception becomes increasingly concerning with age and cardiovascular risk.
In commonly used eligibility criteria, women aged 35 years or older who smoke may face substantial restrictions on combined hormonal contraception, especially with heavier smoking.
Assess:
Age.
Cigarettes smoked per day.
Blood pressure.
Migraine history.
Previous thrombosis.
Other cardiovascular risks.
Preferred alternatives to consider: copper IUD, LNG-IUS, implant or progestogen-only pill.
HIV infection itself does not automatically prohibit hormonal contraception. However, certain antiretroviral medicines interact with contraceptive hormones.
Ask about the specific regimen and assess:
Drug interactions.
Other medical conditions.
Pregnancy plans.
STI prevention.
Whether condoms are desired alongside a highly effective contraceptive method.
Condoms remain important for STI prevention and may provide additional protection against unintended pregnancy.
For a patient taking efavirenz or another interacting medicine, check current drug-interaction guidance before choosing an implant or oral hormonal method.
The severity and type of liver disease matter.
Severe or decompensated liver disease: hormonal method eligibility may be restricted.
Hepatocellular adenoma or certain liver tumours: hormonal contraception may be contraindicated or require specialist assessment.
Stable, uncomplicated liver disease: some methods may remain suitable.
A copper IUD may be an option where hormonal methods are unsuitable.
Do not apply the same rule to all liver conditions; check the diagnosis and current medical eligibility criteria.
This table is a revision aid, not a substitute for formal eligibility criteria.

rows: Severe hypertension or vascular disease makes combined hormonal contraception unsuitable
IUDs, implant or other eligible progestogen-only methods
Check interactions with implant and pills
Avoid hormonal contraception unless specialist guidance indicates otherwise
IUDs, implant and other eligible methods
Assess combined cardiovascular and VTE risks
Combined hormonal contraception may be contraindicated
Eligibility depends on the specific diagnosis

subsections.subsection_title: How to present your recommendation in an OSCE

blocks.text: Use this four-part structure:
Identify the risk: “Your history of migraine with aura means that oestrogen-containing contraception would increase your stroke risk.”
Explain the restriction: “For that reason, I would not recommend the combined pill, patch or vaginal ring.”
Offer alternatives: “We can consider an implant, a progestogen-only pill or an intrauterine device, depending on your preferences and medical history.”
Make a shared decision: “Would you prefer a long-acting method or one you can stop yourself?”
This demonstrates clinical reasoning rather than simply memorising contraindications.
Q1. What are the four medical eligibility categories?
Category 1: no restriction; Category 2: benefits generally outweigh risks; Category 3: risks generally outweigh benefits; Category 4: unacceptable health risk.
Q2. Which contraceptive method is contraindicated in migraine with aura?
Combined hormonal contraception, including the combined pill, patch and vaginal ring.
Q3. Why should enzyme-inducing medicines be considered before prescribing an implant?
They may accelerate hormone metabolism and reduce contraceptive effectiveness.
Q4. Can a woman with hypertension use contraception?
Yes. Many methods remain available. The method must be selected according to blood pressure, vascular risk and the relevant eligibility criteria.
Q5. Can a woman with diabetes use an IUD?
Yes, an IUD may be appropriate. Assess the type of diabetes, vascular complications, other medical conditions and individual eligibility.
Q6. Is obesity an absolute contraindication to hormonal contraception?
No. Obesity alone does not automatically exclude most methods, although associated cardiovascular and thrombotic risks must be assessed.
Q7. What is the safest approach when a patient has several interacting medical conditions?

Review all conditions and medicines, use current medical eligibility and drug-interaction guidance, and seek specialist advice when needed. Offer a suitable alternative rather than leaving the patient without contraception.
Treating all hormonal contraception as equivalent.
Confusing progestogen-only contraception with combined hormonal contraception.
Failing to ask about migraine aura.
Ignoring drug interactions in epilepsy or HIV.
Recommending combined hormonal contraception without assessing blood pressure and VTE risk.
Assuming obesity alone is a contraindication.
Forgetting to ask about current breast cancer.
Applying a blanket rule to every liver condition.
Failing to respect patient preferences or explain alternatives.
S — Smoking status.
A — Aura with migraine.
F — Factor in previous thrombosis.
E — Evaluate blood pressure.
C — Check current medicines.
H — Hormone-sensitive cancers.
O — Obesity and other cardiovascular risks.
I — Identify diabetes complications.
C — Consider liver disease and other comorbidities.
E — Explain suitable alternatives and agree on a method.
